practice1.prompt: scores.txt sits next to your program. Print every line in it without its newline, then print how many lines there were.

cases.name: prints each score, then the count
the numbers come out of the file, not out of the code

practice1.hint: The lesson's own example builds a string with the lines in it, which is a stand-in for a file rather than a file. The numbers here are on disk, and only open() can reach them.

questions.prompt: What does read() give you back?
choices: The whole file as one string
questions.explain: read() is everything at once. That is fine for a small file and a problem for a large one, which is why the lesson prefers the loop.

questions.prompt: Why does printing the result of readlines() show a blank line between each one?
choices: Each line still carries the newline it had in the file, and print adds another
The file has blank lines in it
questions.explain: The newline is part of the line as it was stored. strip() is what takes it back off.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson call `for line in file:` the best way to read?
choices: It is the shortest to type
It reads one line at a time, so the whole file never has to fit in memory
It is the only way that keeps the order
It closes the file for you
questions.explain: read() and readlines() both load everything. Iterating the file object walks it a line at a time, so a huge file costs no more than a small one.

questions.prompt:
file = open("scores.txt")
for line in file:
    print(line.___())
file.___()
questions.explain: strip() removes the newline the file stored, and close() releases the file once the loop has finished with it.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Say what shape each one hands back, and which of them still works when the file is far too big to hold in memory.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Your pseudocode needs four moves: open the file, walk it a line at a time, test each line, and keep a running count.
